introduction.p: Newton's second law relates force to acceleration, so motion models often involve the second derivative of position. For a mass attached to a spring, the restoring force gives a second-order equation. We will solve constant-coefficient examples and relate their solutions to oscillation and damping.

subsection.title: Simple harmonic motion
subsection.p: Imagine a mass attached to a spring on a frictionless table. Pull the mass to the right, let go, and it moves back and forth.
means the mass is at its resting position. Positive y means it is displaced to the right. Negative y means it is displaced to the left.
A spring obeying Hooke’s law pulls back toward equilibrium:
The constant k measures the stiffness of the spring. The minus sign is the important part. If y>0, the force is negative. If y<0, the force is positive. The force always points back toward 0.

p.me: \text{acceleration is proportional to displacement, but in the opposite direction.}

subsection.p: That is the mathematical heart of simple harmonic motion.

exercise.title: Why do vibrating systems lead to second-order equations?

statement.p: Hooke’s law gives a force F=-ky, and Newton’s second law converts force into acceleration. In your own words, why does that produce y''+\omega^2 y=0, and what sentence about acceleration and displacement is the heart of simple harmonic motion?

hint.p: Acceleration is the second derivative. The restoring force points opposite the displacement, so acceleration is proportional to displacement but in the opposite direction.

subsection.title: The equation y''+\omega^2y=0
subsection.p: has sine and cosine solutions because their second derivatives are negative multiples of themselves.
Since the equation is linear, any linear combination is also a solution:
The constants are determined by two initial conditions. A second-order equation needs two starting values because motion needs both position and velocity.

paragraphs.title: Energy check
paragraphs.p: The undamped spring keeps oscillating because no energy is lost.
The first term is kinetic energy. The second is spring potential energy.
The energy moves back and forth between motion and spring stretch. It does not disappear.

exercise.title: Why does a second-order equation need two starting values?

statement.p: The general solution y=C_1\cos(\omega t)+C_2\sin(\omega t) has two constants. In your own words, why is position alone not enough to determine the future of a spring, and what second piece of initial data is required?

hint.p: Motion needs both where the mass is and how fast it is moving. A mass at equilibrium may stay there or pass through with high speed.

paragraphs.title: Energy with damping
paragraphs.p: Energy decreases, except at instants when y'=0. The damping term drains energy from the motion.

exercise.title: How does damping change the energy?

statement.p: Without friction, energy moves back and forth between motion and spring stretch. With a damping term -cy', oscillations typically shrink. In your own words, why does a force that opposes velocity drain energy, and what role does the decaying exponential envelope play?

hint.p: Damping resists velocity, so it does negative work. The factor e^{-\beta t} shrinks the oscillating amplitude.

note.title: Resonance, first view
note.p: A system resonates when the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency. The forcing then reinforces the natural motion instead of fighting it.

subsection.p: Real systems have damping, so the amplitude does not grow forever. But the warning survives: forcing near the natural frequency can create a much larger response than forcing far from it.

warning.title: Model warning
warning.p: predicts unbounded growth at resonance because it ignores damping and structural limits. It is a warning model, not a complete physical description.

subsection.p: Second-order equations already show that the state of a system may need more than one number. A spring is not determined by position alone. To know what happens next, we also need velocity.
That idea leads naturally to systems of differential equations.

exercise.title: What does it mean for a driven oscillator to resonate?

statement.p: When the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency, the undamped response amplitude can become large. In your own words, why does that happen, and why is the unbounded-growth model a warning rather than a complete physical description?

hint.p: Forcing then reinforces the natural motion instead of fighting it. Real systems have damping and structural limits, so amplitude does not grow forever.
